## Sea-level rise and coastal inundation

### Sea-level rise

Sea-level rise (SLR) is increasing the frequency of tidal "nuisance inundation" or "sunny day flooding" of coastal paths and streets ([Hanslow et al., 2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10113-023-02138-8)). Events that were once considered acute nuisances are now evolving into chronic, recurring issues.  

In addition to tidal flooding, the combination of a major storm surge and high tides, known as a [storm tide](https://www.undrr.org/understanding-disaster-risk/terminology/hips/mh0704), can exacerbate coastal flooding, leading to the possibility of [major](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/flood_awareness_flooding) inundation or catastrophic flooding of coastal buildings and infrastructure. 

Rare storm tide events are traditionally defined as 100-year events with a 1% annual exceedance probability (AEP). This means there is a 1% chance (or a 1 in 100 chance) that an event of a specific magnitude, or a larger one, will happen in any single year. It is possible (but very unlikely) that a 1% AEP event could occur in consecutive years or multiple times within the same year. However, SLR is amplifying the frequency and likelihood of these events. What were once acute, rare major events are projected to become more frequent, chronic major problems in the coming decades.  

### Coastal inundation

Defining the threshold for chronic coastal inundation (e.g., 30 days per year or 3 events over 30 years) depends on the ability of affected systems, whether natural or community-built, to adapt to these impacts.  

The map below examines storm tide flooding over two 30-year periods: the past 30 years before 2025 (1995–2024) and the next 30 years from 2025 (2025–2054). By comparing the two periods and seeing how the colours on the maps change, it highlights the potential increase in significant storm tide events due to sea-level rise, helping to identify locations where chronic coastal inundation issues may emerge and require adaptation planning.

### How to interpret information on the map

Zoom in and out to focus on specific areas around Western Port. Use the layers control to select timeframes or switch basemaps view (OpenStreetMap or Satellite). The legend explains the color-coded number of flood years for the 30 year periods, ranging from frequent (light blue) to less frequent (magenta). A flood year is any year in which storm tide water levels rise above the land surface, making flooding likely. For example, land under the magenta colour experiance between 0 and 5 flood years over the 30 year period. Click on green circle markers to view detailed historic flood-year plots for each location.  

```{r setup, include=FALSE, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width=10, fig.height=7)
```


```{r load packages, include=FALSE}
#https://julianog.github.io/map_flood_years/FloodYearsDemo.html
require(terra)
require(leaflet)
require(purrr)
require(htmltools)
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
voi = vect("Ramsar/") #inundation tiles
voi = voi[voi$RAMSAR_NAM == "Western Port",]
```

```{r read in the tiles, include=FALSE}
xs = list.files("FloodYears_tiles/",full.names = TRUE)

voi_id  = sapply(strsplit(xs,"_"),function(x) substr(x[5],1,4))

xs = xs[voi_id < 4000 & !is.na(voi_id) & voi_id != 3064]
voi_id = voi_id[voi_id < 4000 & !is.na(voi_id) & voi_id != 3064]

voi_id  = sapply(strsplit(xs,"_"),function(x) substr(x[5],1,4))

rl = lapply(xs,function(x) rast(x))

ll = sapply(rl,function(x) geom(centroids(vect(ext(x))))[3:4])

group_name  = sapply(strsplit(xs,"_"),function(x) x[4])


dat <- data.frame(voi_id = voi_id, lat = ll[2,],lon = ll[1,],Name = voi_id)
```


```{r plot the tiles, include=FALSE}


# Define a color palette for the raster
pal <- colorBin((c("magenta", "darkblue", "cyan", "lightblue")), 
                    values(rl[[1]]), na.color = "transparent",bins = 6)

#previewColors(pal)

# Create a leaflet map with both OSM and satellite basemaps
map <- leaflet(dat) %>%
  addTiles(group = "OpenStreetMap") %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldImagery, group = "Satellite") %>%
  addPolygons(data = voi, 
              color = "blue", 
              fillColor = "lightblue", 
              fillOpacity = 0.1, 
              weight = 2,
              group = "Western Port Ramsar")

# Add all raster images with a loop
map <- reduce(seq_along(rl), function(m, i) {
  m %>% addRasterImage(rl[[i]], colors = pal, opacity = 1, group = group_name[i])
}, .init = map)

#map <- map %>%
#  addCircleMarkers(
#    ~lon, ~lat,  # Use your lat/lon columns
#    popup = ~paste0(
#      #"<b>", Name, "</b><br>",
#      "<img src='https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JulianOG/map_flood_years/refs/heads/main/plots/island_floodyears_1981-2020_",voi_id,".png' ",
#      "style='max-width:400px; height:auto; display:block;'>"
#      ),
#    label = ~Name,
##    radius = 3,
#    color = "green",
#    fillOpacity = 0.1,
#    group = "Virtual Gauges"
#  )

# Add legend
map <- map %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = values(rl[[1]]), 
            title = HTML("Number of<br>storm tide<br>exceedence years"),opacity =1)

# Add layers control to switch between basemaps
map <- map %>%
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Satellite","OpenStreetMap"),
    overlayGroups =  c("1995-2024","2025-2054","Western Port Ramsar"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE, mutuallyExclusiveGroups = c("1995-2024","2025-2054"))
  )

# Display the map


map <- map %>%
  hideGroup(c("2025-2054"))  # Ensure this group is hidden initially

```



```{r, echo=FALSE}
map

```


**DISCLAIMER: This work has very limited validation/calibration and shouldn't be used for planning, policy, or navigation. Water levels and digital elevations vertical datumns were aligned by tuning water levels to the number of historic flooding years (1981-2020) for only a few known hotspot locations. As flood history isn't widely accessible, further work is required to obtain local knowledge of historical flooding for each of location with elevation data.**
